name: Crescent Bay Tower

gallery.caption: Podium deck reinforcement, tied out before the pour
Erection sequence walked through on site

blurb: A 28-storey office tower on soft coastal ground, framed to ride a magnitude 7 event with its core intact.
overview: Crescent Bay sits on reclaimed ground within a mile of the fault trace, which put seismic demand, not gravity, in charge of every member size. We ran a buckling-restrained braced frame against a full non-linear time history, tuned the core wall to take the drift, and drove the foundations through liquefiable fill to competent material. The tower went up over a parking structure that stayed open throughout.

name: Palm Ridge Outpatient Pavilion

gallery.caption: Structure poured alongside the running clinic
Fit-out coordinated floor by floor

blurb: An outpatient pavilion built hard against a working clinic, with every consulting room in use throughout.
overview: The pavilion shares a wall, a plant room and an ambulance route with a clinic that could not lose a single room. Noise, vibration and infection control governed the programme more than the structure did: heavy work ran nights, the tie-in to the central plant was staged across four two-hour windows, and every penetration was sealed and pressure-tested before the shift ended.

name: Mesa Civic Hall Retrofit

gallery.caption: Shear wall reinforcement threaded through the old frame
Occupied floors kept open behind hoarding

blurb: A 1971 concrete frame strengthened to current code and given two more floors, with staff at their desks throughout.
overview: The existing frame had capacity nobody had ever calculated, so we started with a laser scan, core samples and a load test rather than an assumption. Strengthening was targeted at fourteen columns and two transfer beams, which was enough to carry the new floors and the code-level drift without touching the occupied levels. Work ran floor by floor behind temporary partitions.

name: Vista Bay Tank Terminal

gallery.caption: Shell courses going up by shell jacking
Seam welding under cover

blurb: Four API 650 tanks, their containment and the manifold that ties them in, built inside a terminal that never stopped shipping.
overview: Two tanks came down and four went up on the same footprint, with the terminal loading trucks through the whole programme. Ring wall foundations were designed for liquefiable fill with stone columns beneath; shells were built by the shell-jacking method to keep the welding at ground level. Every seam was vacuum-box and radiograph tested, and the manifold was hydrotested before the first tie-in was cut.

name: Sierra Vista Cogeneration Plant

gallery.caption: Switchyard structures set and bussed
Transformer landed on its pad

blurb: A combined-cycle plant and its switchyard, tied into a transmission line that stayed energised throughout.
overview: The plant adds 48 MW and a heat recovery loop to a site that already exports power, so the connection could not be dropped for longer than a single planned window. Structures sit on drilled piers below the active zone of soils that swell through a forty degree annual range. Steel was galvanised and match-marked in the shop, and energisation was staged bay by bay against the live line.

name: Sable Ridge Platform Tieback

gallery.caption: Saturation bell on the moon pool
Habitat welding on the riser clamp

blurb: A subsea tieback and riser clamp repair at 412 feet, welded dry inside a habitat by a saturation dive team.
overview: Inspection found fatigue cracking in two riser clamps on a fixed platform, in water too deep and too cold for a wet weld to meet the class. We designed the repair around a welding habitat: the clamp was dewatered, preheated and welded dry, to AWS D3.6M class A, by a saturation team living at depth for eighteen days. Every pass was video-logged and ultrasonically verified before the habitat came off.

facts.v: AWS D3.6M class A, dry habitat

name: Kestrel Field Turnaround

gallery.caption: Spool fit-up under a weld tent
Onshore fabrication ahead of the window

blurb: A process upgrade with 38 tie-ins into live systems, executed inside an eleven-day window offshore.
overview: The upgrade needed 38 cuts into systems that could only be opened during the annual shutdown, on a platform where every tonne of spare deck space had to be booked in advance. Spools were fabricated, tested and laid down in erection order onshore, each tie-in was rehearsed against the scan-registered model, and the sequence was written so no two cuts competed for the same crane.

name: Harborside Jetty Rebuild

gallery.caption: Underdeck survey before the repair scheme
Dive control on the barge alongside

blurb: Rebuilding a fuel jetty and repairing 186 piles beneath it, without taking the berth out of service.
overview: Deepening to take a larger class of vessel undermined the existing pile embedment, so every pile in the affected bay needed a jacket and a structural weld before the dredger could pass. Dive crews worked surface-supplied between vessel calls, welding wet to class B where the repair allowed and setting habitats where it did not. The jetty handled ships through the entire programme.

name: Canyon Ridge Logistics Centre

gallery.caption: Frame erection, bay by bay
Platform and pads ahead of the steel

blurb: A portal framed distribution centre taken from ground investigation to handover in sixteen months.
overview: A large shed is a simple structure with an unforgiving programme. Connections were detailed to the fabricator's shop standards rather than a generic library, steel arrived in erection sequence, and the slab was poured in bays that followed the frame rather than the other way round. The ground beneath it needed 40,000 cubic yards of engineered fill before any of that could start.

name: Coyote Creek Crossing

gallery.caption: Deck reinforcement over the falsework
Setting out checked against the survey

blurb: A three-span replacement crossing built over a flood control channel that has to stay clear through storm season.
overview: The existing crossing was scour-critical and two lanes short. The replacement is a three-span prestressed girder bridge on drilled shafts set back from the channel, so nothing new stands in the waterway. Falsework had to be out of the channel before each storm season, which set the pour sequence, and traffic stayed on the old structure until the new one carried load.

name: Arroyo Seco Levee Works

gallery.caption: Culvert walls poured in sections
Haul road and channel works running together

blurb: Three miles of levee raised and re-armoured, with the channel kept live through two storm seasons.
overview: The levee was built to a rainfall record that no longer holds. We modelled the channel against the flow it will see in fifty years, raised and re-armoured three miles of embankment, and rebuilt eleven outfall structures along it. Everything in the channel had to be out or flood-ready by the first of November each year, which set the programme more than any other constraint.

name: Seabright Outfall Repair

gallery.caption: Survey spread on the support vessel
Diver on the repaired section

blurb: A damaged subsea outfall located, clamped and welded in place, with the discharge never taken off line.
overview: A dropped anchor had dented and cracked a section of outfall in 90 feet of water. We surveyed the full run by ROV, designed a split clamp that could be set and welded by divers against a live flow, and installed it in four dive days. Post-repair ultrasonic testing and a pressure survey confirmed the line back to full rated flow.

facts.v: Split clamp, wet weld class B
